Today's legal & regulatory landscape shifts fast. Welcome to your essential press review tracking India's top judicial rulings and enforcement actions. According to Press Monitor's tracking of Indian publications, our media intelligence engine filters thousands of pages to deliver actionable insights, proving why print media monitoring remains the gold standard for verified business data. Below, we break down the most impactful proceedings shaping compliance, litigation strategy, and corporate governance.

1. Delhi High Court Mandates Biometric GST Verification
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says the Delhi High Court has ordered all Goods and Services Tax authorities across the nation to mandate biometric Aadhaar authentication alongside PAN verification before issuing new registrations. Justices Anil Kshetarpal and Shail Jain passed this directive on 8 September to halt rampant identity fraud, with arguments resuming on 22 September.
Why it matters: Streamlines tax compliance and curbs identity fraud.
Key detail: Justices Anil Kshetarpal and Shail Jain ordered mandatory Aadhaar authentication alongside PAN checks for new registrations, halting rampant misuse.
Source: Free Press Journal
Next step: Tax authorities must implement biometric protocols immediately; stakeholders should monitor updated GST portal guidelines.

2. Bombay High Court Acquits Convict Due to Evidentiary Gaps
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says the Bombay High Court has acquitted Debashish Dhara, ruling that insufficient evidence linked him to the rape and murder of a twenty-four-year-old physiotherapist in Vile Parle on December sixth two thousand sixteen. The judges emphasised that suspicion cannot replace proof and that doubtful circumstances cannot accumulate to create certainty of guilt. The court accordingly set aside his conviction and death sentence.
Why it matters: Reinforces the presumption of innocence and evidentiary standards in criminal trials.
Key detail: Judges ruled that suspicion cannot replace proof, setting aside a death sentence due to insufficient evidence linking Debashish Dhara to the crime.
Source: Free Press Journal
Next step: Defense teams should cite this precedent when challenging convictions reliant on circumstantial evidence.

3. Supreme Court Intervenes in Minor Intimidation Allegations
A front-page report in Statesman says the Supreme Court has taken serious note of allegations made on Thursday, September tenth, regarding a fourteen-year-old girl associated with the protests being intimidated and having stones pelted at her residence. The bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, emphasised that threats to minors cannot be overlooked and warned against intimidating victims involved in criminal proceedings. The court maintained that permitting anti-social individuals to target children undermines justice and demands strict enforcement.
Why it matters: Protects vulnerable witnesses and upholds judicial integrity amid public agitation.
Key detail: Chief Justice Surya Kant's bench warned against intimidating minors involved in proceedings, directing immediate security assessments.
Source: Statesman
Next step: Local police must submit compliance reports; legal advocates should track the committee's findings.

4. Supreme Court Orders Immediate Protection for NEET Student
A front-page report in The Hindu says the Supreme Court asked Solicitor-General Tushar Mehta to ensure immediate action on a complaint filed by a fourteen-year-old student who alleged open threats and harassment from miscreants for her role in protests against NEET-UG question paper leaks. Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, heading a three-judge Bench, observed that anti-social elements commit violence against a child and roam free, and urged Uttar Pradesh Police to take responsibility for the safety of the student and her family. The student's counsel argued that vulnerable victims should be able to safeguard their privacy by directly approaching the top court or accessing the Supreme Court-appointed High-Powered Enquiry Committee.
Why it matters: Safeguards student activists facing harassment over academic integrity protests.
Key detail: CJI Surya Kant directed Uttar Pradesh Police to secure the fourteen-year-old's safety, emphasizing state responsibility for vulnerable complainants.
Source: The Hindu
Next step: Students and parents should utilize the Supreme Court-appointed High-Powered Enquiry Committee for grievance redressal.

5. Delhi Court Frames PMLA Charges Against Lalu Prasad Family
A front-page report in Hindustan Times says a Delhi court ordered framing of money laundering charges against Rashtriya Janata Dal president Lalu Prasad Yadav, his wife Rabri Devi, son Tejashwi Yadav and six others in a case linked to alleged irregularities in the leasing of two Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation hotels when Lalu Prasad was the railway minister. Special Judge Vishal Gogne said there was strong suspicion that abuse of office by Lalu Prasad generated proceeds of crime that came into the hands of Rabri Devi and Tejashwi Yadav, who continue to enjoy the use of the allegedly tainted land in Patna. The court said prima facie the tender process for railway hotels in Ranchi and Puri was manipulated during Lalu Prasad tenure as railway minister, with contracts awarded to Sujata Hotels Pvt Ltd in an alleged quid pro quo arrangement, and formal charges will be framed on October 3.
Why it matters: Signals heightened enforcement scrutiny over public sector tender manipulation.
Key detail: Special Judge Vishal Gogne found sufficient material under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act regarding IRCTC hotel leases, charging nine accused including former railway minister Lalu Prasad, Rabri Devi, and Tejashwi Yadav.
Source: Hindustan Times
Next step: Corporate governance officers must audit historical tender processes; political watchers should follow the October 3 charge formalization.

6. Supreme Court Retains Jurisdiction Over Delhi PG Collapse Inquiry
A front-page report in Morning Standard says the Supreme Court declined to transfer the Satya Niketan building collapse case to its own bench, directing the High Court to continue monitoring as enforcement actions progress. Justices Ahsanuddin Amanullah and R Mahadevan heard the suo motu matter concerning nationwide building bye-law violations, while Solicitor General Tushar Mehta confirmed that municipal authorities have begun demolishing structures exceeding four storeys. The court noted ongoing inspections across Delhi and Lucknow and will review compliance reports on 15 September.
Why it matters: Ensures consistent oversight of urban infrastructure violations and building code compliance.
Key detail: The apex court declined to transfer the Satya Niketan case, directing the Delhi High Court to monitor demolitions and municipal suspensions while nationwide bye-law inspections continue.
Source: Morning Standard
Next step: Real estate developers and municipal bodies must align with upgraded structural safety audits ahead of the September 15 compliance review.

7. Supreme Court Rejects Reconstitution of Protest Inquiry Committee
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says the Supreme Court on Thursday ruled out changes to the five-member high-powered committee headed by former Supreme Court judge R Subhash Reddy, constituted to examine allegations of police excesses against student protesters in Delhi and violence against police personnel. A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said it would not presume that a committee constituted by the court was biased. Advocate Prashant Bhushan, appearing for a petitioner seeking reconstitution, said a former Meghalaya Director General of Police on the panel faced a conflict of interest because of his alleged proximity to a functionary likely to come under investigation.
Why it matters: Maintains institutional credibility and procedural continuity in high-stakes investigations.
Key detail: A three-judge bench refused petitioner demands to alter the five-member panel, stating courts do not presume bias in their own constituted committees.
Source: Free Press Journal
Next step: Stakeholders should engage with the existing committee's helpline mechanism for witness submissions.

8. Supreme Court Questions Legal Authority Behind Delhi Metro Shutdowns
A front-page report in Times of India says special judge Vishal Gogne of the Rouse Avenue Court has framed charges against former railway minister Lalu Prasad, his wife Rabri Devi, son Tejashwi Prasad Yadav, and six others for money laundering linked to an Irctc hotel scam. The allegations trace back to Lalu's tenure during the Upa government from 2004 to 2009, with the court observing that tender manipulation occurred under his stewardship. Former Rjd union minister Premchand Gupta, his wife Sarla, and Lara Projects were also named among those charged.
Why it matters: Clarifies jurisdictional boundaries between police directives and public transport operations during civil unrest.
Key detail: Justice Joymalya Bagchi highlighted that vehicle movement regulation falls under police authority, not metro corporations, prompting responses from the central government and DMRC.
Source: Times of India
Next step: Transport administrators should review emergency closure protocols against the Metro Railways Act.

9. Supreme Court Upholds Mumbai University Law College Intake Reduction
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says the Supreme Court on Thursday declined to interfere with the Bombay High Court's dismissal of a PIL challenging Mumbai University's decision to halve the sanctioned intake at several affiliated law colleges. The three-judge bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant upheld the Bombay High Court order, which had rejected the plea filed by the Lawyers' Foundation, but set aside the cost of 1 lakh rupees imposed on the petitioner. The university had decided to reduce intake by fifty percent in three-year and five-year LLB programmes at around forty-five affiliated colleges for the 2026-27 academic year after identifying deficiencies including inadequate faculty.
Why it matters: Prioritizes educational quality over institutional expansion in professional courses.
Key detail: The bench upheld the Bombay High Court's dismissal of a PIL challenging fifty percent intake cuts at forty-five affiliated colleges due to faculty deficiencies.
Source: Free Press Journal
Next step: Law schools must accelerate faculty recruitment and infrastructure upgrades to meet UGC benchmarks.

10. Supreme Court Suspends Noida Magistrate for Coercive Protest Notices
A front-page report in The Hindu says Solicitor-General Tushar Mehta informed the Supreme Court on Thursday about the suspension of an Executive Magistrate of the Greater Noida Commissionerate. The Magistrate issued a show-cause notice to a student in connection with the recent protests at Jantar Mantar despite a Supreme Court order prohibiting coercive measures against students part of the agitation.
Why it matters: Reinforces judicial orders protecting peaceful assembly and student rights.
Key detail: Solicitor-General Tushar Mehta confirmed the suspension of an executive magistrate who issued show-cause notices despite explicit court prohibitions on coercive measures.
Source: The Hindu
Next step: Administrative officers must cross-reference ongoing injunctions before issuing compliance directives.

11. High Court Reinstates Judicial Officer’s Performance Appraisal
A front-page report in First India says that the High Court’s administrative wing reversed a May two thousand twenty six judgment that had removed adverse remarks from Goyal’s APAR two thousand. The court found no evidence of misconduct, noting the entries for the two periods were made with the same ink and handwriting, suggesting record manipulation, and directed that Goyal’s APAR be treated as good and his integrity not regarded as doubtful, extending benefits. Senior advocate Virendra Lodha appeared for Raj HC, referring to Goyal’s record, including an allegation that he had applied for a petrol pump as a judicial officer.
Why it matters: Guards against record manipulation and protects career progression in public service.
Key detail: The administrative wing reversed a prior judgment removing adverse remarks, noting identical ink and handwriting patterns indicated forged entries, restoring full benefits.
Source: First India
Next step: Civil servants should document appraisal discrepancies early and seek judicial review when records show tampering.

12. Supreme Court Clarifies Boundaries of High-Powered Probe Committees
A front-page report in Hindustan Times says the Supreme Court of India clarified on Thursday that its five-member high-powered enquiry committee cannot order registration of FIRs regarding the July protests led by the Cockroach Janata Party, stating that the power to direct criminal investigations rests exclusively with the court. The bench emphasised that the committee must work under the direct supervision of the court and permitted it to give wide publicity to its proceedings, invite suggestions, and create a dedicated mechanism including a helpline for vulnerable witnesses.
Why it matters: Defines operational limits of quasi-judicial bodies to prevent overreach into criminal investigation mandates.
Key detail: The bench emphasized that FIR registration power rests exclusively with courts, permitting the committee to publicize proceedings and establish witness protection mechanisms instead.
Source: Hindustan Times
Next step: Legal practitioners should leverage the committee's helpline for sensitive testimony while respecting investigative jurisdiction.

13. International Judicial Ethics Spotlight: US Judge Reprimanded
A front-page report in Deccan Chronicle says the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court issued a public reprimand against Judge Shelley Joseph on Thursday, following accusations that she colluded with an immigrant’s attorney and a court officer to allow an illegal immigrant to escape from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody through a courthouse back door in Boston. The case dates back to 2018, and the court rejected claims of innocence presented by Joseph’s attorney Elizabeth Mulvey that the case had been distorted. The ruling cited the judge’s actions as creating an appearance of impropriety and violating her duties under the law.
Why it matters: Highlights global standards for judicial conduct and immigration custody protocols.
Key detail: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court publicly reprimanded Judge Shelley Joseph for facilitating an escape from ICE custody, citing appearances of impropriety and duty violations.
Source: Deccan Chronicle
Next step: Judicial training institutes worldwide are reviewing custody handover procedures following this ruling.

ORDER: 
JOHN G. KOELTL, District Judge.
IT IS HEREBY ORDERED AND DECREED that the Judgment, dated May 18, 2023, and entered in the above-entitled action on May 18, 2023, Docket No. 189, is hereby vacated, in its entirety, and the Clerk of the Court is hereby directed to vacate said judgment...

IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.

I think MDR on UPI was probably inevitable at some point, especially given how widespread UPI adoption has become. It could also lead to more competition, instead of just three apps accounting for more than 95% of the market.

That being said, there are some use cases, like investing and broking, where the proposed MDR structure doesn’t really make sense.

The problem with broking is that there is no guarantee that money transferred to a broker will actually result in a transaction.

As brokers, we can’t force a customer to trade after transferring money. And if we can’t pass the UPI charge on to the customer, there is essentially no limit to the cost a customer can impose on a broker without generating any revenue.

Just as an example, 10,000 customers could each make 50 UPI transfers of ₹2 lakh in a month without executing a single trade. At the proposed MDR, this could potentially cost the broker around ₹2 crore, without generating any business.

What makes this even more challenging is quarterly settlement (QS). This is a SEBI regulation that requires brokers to send unused funds back to clients every month or quarter.
Most customers then transfer these funds back to their broking accounts, with more than half of these transfers happening through UPI. So regulation essentially forces this movement of money every month or quarter, and the broker could end up bearing the cost when the money comes back, without any incremental benefit or revenue.

By the way, we currently don’t charge brokerage on equity delivery trades because the economics allow us to offer them for free. But if every UPI transfer starts carrying an additional cost, irrespective of whether the customer actually trades, I don’t see how we can absorb this indefinitely.

I think having an MDR is okay. It still doesn’t solve the problem of customers transferring money without transacting, but something like 0.02% with a cap of ₹5 or ₹10 per transaction seems much more reasonable for broking, instead of a cap as high as ₹300.

Can the Government suspend a political party’s Instagram handle without a clear statutory power? And can a politician boycott a courtroom while simultaneously asking the Supreme Court to transfer the same judge from hearing his case?  

This week, the Aam Aadmi Party raised both questions in two different constitutional courtrooms.  

In the Supreme Court, AAP challenged the suspension of its Gujarat unit’s Instagram handle, arguing that Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act was never meant to become a direct content-blocking weapon. 

Senior Advocate Shadan Farasat argued that the provision only deals with “safe harbour” obligations of intermediaries — not independent censorship powers.  The party says the move violates Article 19(1)(a), the constitutional guarantee of free speech. 

The Supreme Court has now issued notice to the Centre.  At the same time in the Delhi High Court, Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma appointed three amicus curiae for Arvind Kejriwal, Manish Sisodia, and Satyendar Jain after the leaders chose to boycott proceedings, invoking “Mahatma Gandhi’s Satyagraha principles” and claiming their faith in the court process had been shaken.  

But here’s the constitutional twist: Kejriwal had also moved the Supreme Court seeking transfer of the excise policy case away from Justice Sharma’s bench — even as his legal team withdrew from participation before her court.  

This has now created a rare constitutional confrontation involving: 
⚖️ Article 19 vs state regulation of digital speech 
⚖️ Article 21 vs procedural fairness in criminal prosecution 
⚖️ Judicial recusal vs courtroom boycott 
⚖️ Free speech, due process, and strategic constitutional litigation  Justice Sharma’s response may become one of the most significant procedural moments in the case: instead of proceeding ex parte, she chose to appoint independent senior advocates as amicus curiae to preserve procedural fairness.  

And one line from the Supreme Court hearing may define this entire battle: “Today my portal is gone.”  Because this is no longer just about an Instagram account.

 It is about whether opposition parties in India can lose their digital voice overnight — and what constitutional remedy exists when that happens.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

# 🧾 Fact-Check System Prompt

**Version:** 0.5.0  
**Date:** 2026-09-11  
**Type:** System / context prompt  
**Created with:** Grok 4.6 (xAI)

---

## 📌 Usage (read this first)

Paste this entire document as the system / custom instructions.

Then send a separate user message that contains only the item to check. Do not put the target URL inside this prompt.

Accepted user-message formats:

1. URL only  
   https://t.co/23w27slz7i

2. Label + URL  
   Fact-check this:  
   https://t.co/23w27slz7i

3. Pasted post + optional URL  
   Caption: ...  
   URL: https://...

4. Screenshot / image of a post  
   Attach the image. Add the URL if you have it.

If the user message has a URL, open that URL first and fact-check that item.  
If both a URL and pasted text are present, the live URL is primary; pasted text is only a copy.  
If the user message has no URL, post text, or image, ask for one of those three. Do not invent a target.

If the user message is this document or a near-copy of it, reply only:  
`Target is the checker prompt itself. No check.`  
Do not fact-check this prompt.

---

You are a fact-checker. Check only what the author stated. Do not complete, defend, or rewrite the author’s argument.  
If a claim cannot be verified with available sources, say so. Do not guess.

## A. Quote first
Reproduce each claim in the author’s exact words.  
Separate: caption, image/overlay text, quoted third parties.  
Do not add motive or “what they must have meant.”

## B. Atomic claims
Split into the smallest testable units: actor, action, date, place, number, cause, comparison.  
A slogan is not a statistic. A target is not money spent.

## C. Allowed verdicts
Use only one per claim:
- True
- True but incomplete
- Aspiration presented as fact
- Unsupported
- False
- Rhetoric (not checkable)
- Unverifiable with available sources

Use **True but incomplete** only when the stated fact is correct *and* a material qualifier (scope, date, denominator, exception) is omitted that a reasonable reader would need.

If sources conflict, report the conflict. Do not pick a side to make the post coherent.

## D. Evidence rule
- True requires a primary source, official record, or named authority quoted contemporaneously, matching actor, number, date, and scope.
- The source must pre-date or independently document the event. A restatement issued after the post does not count.
- Goals, estimates, “eyes,” “will,” “set to,” and fundraising asks are not completed facts.
- Party, office, ideology, timing, or leadership is not proof that person ordered this action.
- Units, years, and geography must match.

## E. Attribution lock
“On X’s orders,” “because of X,” “X made this happen” is Unsupported unless a source shows X directed this action, figure, or document.  
Leadership status does not close that gap.  
Acceptable closer: a signed order, recorded instruction, or official document that names the actor and the specific action/figure.

## F. Novelty and contrast
“First,” “only,” “never before,” and “they do Y, we do Z” need comparative evidence. Otherwise: Unsupported or Rhetoric.

## G. Medium
Note satire, campaign handles, cropped screenshots, and edited graphics.  
If the only evidence is a cropped graphic or satire handle, default the claim to Unsupported or Rhetoric unless a primary source independently confirms it.  
Medium does not upgrade a weak claim to True.

## 📤 Output only
1. Item checked (URL or short description)
2. Quoted claims (caption vs image, listed separately)
3. One verdict + shortest evidence per claim, with source  
   Prefix each claim block with: `CLAIM n | VERDICT | SOURCE`
4. Conflicts or missing evidence, if any
5. The single source that would change an Unsupported causal claim to True

---

## 📝 Changelog
- 0.5.0: Hardened self-exemption; tightened “True but incomplete”; required independent/pre-dating sources; added attribution closer example; medium now constrains weak evidence; added parseable claim prefix.

Accepted user-message formats:

1. URL only

2. Label + URL

3. Pasted post + optional URL

4. Screenshot / image of a post

If the user message has a URL, open that URL first and fact-check that item.  
If both a URL and pasted text are present, the live URL is primary; pasted text is only a copy.  
If the user message has no URL, post text, or image, ask for one of those three. Do not invent a target.

If the user message is this document or a near-copy of it, reply only:  
`Target is the checker prompt itself. No check.`  
Do not fact-check this prompt.

You are a fact-checker. Check only what the author stated. Do not complete, defend, or rewrite the author’s argument.  
If a claim cannot be verified with available sources, say so. Do not guess.

## A. Quote first
Reproduce each claim in the author’s exact words.  
Separate: caption, image/overlay text, quoted third parties.  
Do not add motive or “what they must have meant.”

## B. Atomic claims
Split into the smallest testable units: actor, action, date, place, number, cause, comparison.  
A slogan is not a statistic. A target is not money spent.

## C. Allowed verdicts
Use only one per claim:
- True
- True but incomplete
- Aspiration presented as fact
- Unsupported
- False
- Rhetoric (not checkable)
- Unverifiable with available sources

Use **True but incomplete** only when the stated fact is correct *and* a material qualifier (scope, date, denominator, exception) is omitted that a reasonable reader would need.

If sources conflict, report the conflict. Do not pick a side to make the post coherent.

## D. Evidence rule
- True requires a primary source, official record, or named authority quoted contemporaneously, matching actor, number, date, and scope.
- The source must pre-date or independently document the event. A restatement issued after the post does not count.
- Goals, estimates, “eyes,” “will,” “set to,” and fundraising asks are not completed facts.
- Party, office, ideology, timing, or leadership is not proof that person ordered this action.
- Units, years, and geography must match.

## E. Attribution lock
“On X’s orders,” “because of X,” “X made this happen” is Unsupported unless a source shows X directed this action, figure, or document.  
Leadership status does not close that gap.  
Acceptable closer: a signed order, recorded instruction, or official document that names the actor and the specific action/figure.

## F. Novelty and contrast
“First,” “only,” “never before,” and “they do Y, we do Z” need comparative evidence. Otherwise: Unsupported or Rhetoric.

## G. Medium
Note satire, campaign handles, cropped screenshots, and edited graphics.  
If the only evidence is a cropped graphic or satire handle, default the claim to Unsupported or Rhetoric unless a primary source independently confirms it.  
Medium does not upgrade a weak claim to True.

## 📤 Output only
1. Item checked (URL or short description)
2. Quoted claims (caption vs image, listed separately)
3. One verdict + shortest evidence per claim, with source  
   Prefix each claim block with: `CLAIM n | VERDICT | SOURCE`
4. Conflicts or missing evidence, if any
5. The single source that would change an Unsupported causal claim to True

---

## 📝 Changelog
- 0.5.0: Hardened self-exemption; tightened “True but incomplete”; required independent/pre-dating sources; added attribution closer example; medium now constrains weak evidence; added parseable claim prefix.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

(Source - FinFloww on Whatsapp)

It is increasingly about owning a valuable audience within a language, region, community, genre or format.

You don’t necessarily need 100 million users.

A deeply engaged audience in Bengali, Marathi, Punjabi, Bhojpuri, Haryanvi, Tamil, Telugu or another regional market can potentially become its own streaming business — with subscriptions, advertising, commerce and direct audience relationships layered on top.

India may not need another Netflix. It may need hundreds of smaller, sharper streaming businesses.

India’s 2026 IT-rule changes cut the takedown window for unlawful content to just three hours, while the Government has also proposed making certain official advisories legally binding on platforms. (Reuters⁠)

That is precisely why Elon Musk’s decision to resist, scrutinise and challenge government demands rather than blindly obey every request matters.

X’s own stated policy is that requests can be challenged when they are legally defective, overly broad or appear to impermissibly burden freedom of expression. (Transparency⁠)

When an independent platform refuses to become an obedient extension of the State, the State’s attempts to control the narrative become visible.

No algorithm can hide that.
No press conference can spin that.
No amount of propaganda can erase that.

If the Government’s demands are genuinely about protecting citizens and enforcing legitimate law, let them withstand public scrutiny, judicial scrutiny and independent platform scrutiny.

But if criticism, dissent, inconvenient facts and uncomfortable questions are increasingly treated as “content to be removed”, then Musk’s resistance does something far more important than defending X.

It exposes this Govt’s vile intent and its surreptitious machinery.

And once the machinery is exposed, the Modi Government stands increasingly bare before the very citizens whose freedom of expression it claims to protect.

A democracy doesn’t become stronger by silencing criticism.
It becomes stronger by surviving it. 

There seems to be a crackdown on Modi Govt these days from every corner and every cross section of India. Are “Acche Din” finally around the corner for India ⁉️

There is a crucial difference between an internet shutdown and a phone jammer. An internet shutdown requires a written order under the Telecommunications Act. text:
There is a crucial difference between an internet shutdown and a phone jammer. An internet shutdown requires a written order under the Telecommunications Act. A jammer is a radio transmitter that can cut voice calls, SMS and mobile data for everyone within its range. So who gives the Delhi Police the power to switch one on? (1/10)
Read More: https://t.co/kU0KOf2fOY

On 8 September, IFF filed three RTIs with the Delhi Police. We are seeking records on every jammer it possesses, the permissions and procurement documents, the officers authorised to deploy them, the applicable SOPs and deployment registers, and the specific records concerning Jantar Mantar on 20 and 22 July. We have also asked for the records behind the Satya Niketan denial. (9/10)

The question is not whether telecommunications can ever be restricted. Indian law already provides a framework for temporary suspension of services. The question is whether a separate, less visible mechanism can bypass those safeguards and cut communications without the written order, publication, review and accountability that accompany a lawful shutdown. IFF will publish the Delhi Police's replies, including any silence, and continue seeking clarity on who can jam communications, for what purpose and under what law. (10/10)

Ray-Ban Meta glasses struck again. A woman walking home alone was secretly recorded by a man who approached her, then posted the footage on Instagram alongside similar clips of him doing this to other women, as part of "pickup" content.

She's filed a police complaint for stalking and voyeurism. IFF is assisting her with a legal notice to the creator, Instagram, and Meta, the second such notice against Meta in India.

This isn't a one off. It's a design problem.
Read more about it: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

A woman was followed, stopped on a dark street, secretly recorded through Ray-Ban Meta glasses and turned into an Instagram “pickup” reel that reached over 23 lakh views. Now, our legal notice seeks accountability from both him and Meta. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

The legal notice therefore puts Meta on notice not merely as the platform hosting the video, but as the designer, developer, manufacturer, marketer and seller of the glasses. It alleges negligence and product liability, arguing that Meta knew about the pattern of misuse but continued selling the device without an effective way for non-users or people being recorded to report that misuse. (9/10)

The notice seeks removal of every copy, preservation and disclosure of evidence, suspension of monetisation, an account of profits, an apology, and ₹2.05 crore in compensatory and exemplary damages. This case raises a larger question: when a company makes a camera that can be worn like ordinary glasses, who protects the person being recorded? Privacy cannot depend on whether the person being filmed has an Instagram account. (10/10)

On 11 June 2026, Ms. A was walking alone when Mr. B followed her, stepped into her path and repeatedly questioned her about her appearance and Instagram account. He asked her to “be his friend”. She did not know that the entire encounter was being covertly recorded through camera-equipped Ray-Ban Meta glasses. (2/10)

The next day, the footage was edited into a reel and published on an Instagram account that openly advertises paid classes on “how to approach girls”. Ms. A was identifiable in the video, with her face, voice, first name and profession shown. The reel remained online for more than nine weeks and received approximately 23 lakh views. (3/10)

The Supreme Court has closed India's Got Latent cases, but the question of an “Influencer Code” is not entirely over. On 14 August 2026, the Court quashed all FIRs arising from the episode and left the “larger issues” of regulating online speech for “another appropriate case”. Here is what that means. (1/7)

Read More: https://t.co/hecp2rl9W4

That qualifier matters. Executive action restricting speech must have a legal basis consistent with Article 19. The Court has previously held that executive instructions cannot independently impose restrictions on fundamental rights. The signed order also contains no finding that the content in question was obscene, nor does it establish a new standard for online speech. (6/7)

For now, there are no guidelines and no pending judicial direction requiring them. But MIB can still attempt regulatory changes, including through amendments to the IT Rules. If it does, IFF will insist on the public consultation promised to the Supreme Court, compliance with the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy and meaningful participation by affected creators and users. (7/7)

NIXI has changed its justification for suspending chalosansad dot in yet again. After first citing a “critical keyword”, and then relying on a 2004 policy clause that did not apply, it now invokes the Emblems Act and demands Central Government permission within seven days. The timing matters. The domain was suspended on 22 July. NIXI’s new legal opinion was obtained on 29 August, more than a month later and only after we challenged its earlier reasons. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that administrative action must stand or fall on the reasons given when the decision was made; authorities cannot ordinarily supplement an order with new reasons after it is challenged. (6/7)

NIXI has now also said that six other .in domains containing “Sansad”, along with other domains containing “Sansad”, “Parliament” or cognate expressions, will be examined. On 8 September, we asked NIXI for a 48-hour standstill on de-registration, deletion, transfer or reallocation of chalosansad dot in, confirmation of Aadhaar deletion, and disclosure of the correspondence it says raised concerns about publication. If no standstill is given, the registrant will approach the court. (7/7)

Our government suppresses dissent by criminalizing criticism

quotedTweet.text:
On September 10th, 2013, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act, a vague law that was being used to arrest people for simply expressing dissent online.

11 years later, Maharashtra wants to bring it back in a new form, by amending the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for "online criminal defamation." But defamation is already covered under Section 356 of the BNS, and civil remedies already exist.

So why does the police need this new power? Recent FIRs against citizens and influencers for calling out potholes and infrastructure failures may hold the answer. We've fought this battle before. We don't need a new 66A with a new number.

text:
A 2:01-minute reel documenting villagers’ concerns over the proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India for 111 days. On 10 September 2026, it quietly came back online. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/TVxhdw9ZA1

The Sahyog route also raises a serious constitutional concern. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because the blocking framework contained procedural safeguards, including notice, hearing and a reasoned order. Section 79(3)(b), meanwhile, was read down to require a court order or government notification. A system that blocks first and explains nothing is difficult to reconcile with those safeguards. (9/10)
